svg.title: Three routes to the same ΔH
svg.desc: An enthalpy diagram sits at the centre. Reactants are drawn on a level at the left, products lower on the right, joined by a direct arrow labelled with the reaction enthalpy. Above both sits a level marked constituent elements in their standard states, reached from the reactants by an arrow equal to minus the sum of their formation enthalpies and leading down to the products by an arrow equal to the sum of the products' formation enthalpies. Going up and over gives the same answer as going straight across, which is exactly why the formation-enthalpy formula works: the reaction enthalpy equals the sum of the products' formation enthalpies minus the sum of the reactants'. Three method panels surround it. The first, tabulated formation enthalpies: use it when a table is given, apply the formula with stoichiometric coefficients, remember that an element in its standard state is zero and that the physical state matters, since liquid water is minus 286 and gaseous water minus 242 kilojoules per mole; this method is exact to the precision of the table. The second, Hess's Law by algebra: use it when you are given two or more reactions rather than a table; reverse an equation and the sign of its enthalpy flips, multiply an equation and its enthalpy multiplies, then add and cancel; also exact. The third, average bond enthalpies: use it when neither a table of formation enthalpies nor a set of reactions is given; the reaction enthalpy is approximately the sum of the bonds broken minus the sum of the bonds formed, remembering that breaking costs energy and forming releases it; this one is only approximate, because the tabulated values are averages over many different molecules, so expect to be out by ten to twenty kilojoules per mole, as in the hydrogenation of ethylene where bond enthalpies give minus 123 against a true value of minus 137. A footer covers calorimetry: the coffee-cup calorimeter is open to the atmosphere and therefore at constant pressure, so the heat it measures is the enthalpy change, computed as mass times specific heat times temperature change, with the sign of the reaction heat opposite that of the solution's; the bomb calorimeter is sealed and therefore at constant volume, so no pressure-volume work is done and the heat it measures is the change in internal energy, computed from the calibrated heat capacity of the whole assembly times the temperature change; and the two are related by the change in enthalpy equalling the change in internal energy plus the change in moles of gas times the gas constant times temperature, so when the moles of gas do not change the two are equal.
svg.text: Three routes to the same ΔH
Enthalpy is a state function, so only the endpoints count. That single fact is why all three methods below are legitimate.
up and over = straight across. ΔH°_rxn = ΣΔH°_f(products) −
when a table of ΔH°_f is given
Element in its standard state = 0. State
when you are given reactions, not a table
Line the equations up so the unwanted
Calorimetry: which device measures which quantity
Coffee cup — open to the air, so constant pressure, so the heat it measures *is* ΔH. q = mcΔT for the solution, and q_rxn =
−q_solution. Bomb — sealed, so constant volume, so w = 0 and the heat it measures is ΔU. q_rxn = −C_cal·ΔT, with C_cal found by
calibration. Converting: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gas·RT, so when the moles of gas do not change, the two are the same number.
Exothermic (ΔH < 0): the flask gets warm — heat has left the system. Endothermic (ΔH > 0): the flask gets cold. The thermometer reads
the surroundings, so its sign is always opposite the reaction's.
